Leave a comment 6 min of reading Hair attributed to Beethoven undergoes genetic sequencing and reveals risk of liver disease, hepatitis B, and a family secret, but one of the most famous locks kept for almost 200 years wasn’t even his and belonged to a woman. Written by Valdemar Medeiros Published on 23/07/2026 at 09:23 Science and Technology Follow us on Google News Be the first to react! 0 0 0 0 0 0 Prefer CPG on Google Listen to this content Researchers analyzed eight hair locks attributed to Ludwig van Beethoven and managed to sequence the composer’s genome from five samples considered authentic. The study revealed a genetic predisposition to liver disease, signs of hepatitis B infection before death, and a historical surprise: the famous Hiller lock, used in previous lead studies, did not belong to Beethoven but to a woman. Ludwig van Beethoven died in 1827, at the age of 56, after suffering for decades from progressive hearing loss, gastrointestinal problems, and severe liver disease. Almost 200 years later, scientists decided to investigate part of this mystery using DNA preserved in hair locks attributed to the composer. The study, published in the scientific journal Current Biology, analyzed eight independent locks attributed to Beethoven. Five of them showed genetic compatibility with each other and were considered almost certainly authentic by the researchers. The analysis revealed a genetic predisposition to liver disease, evidence of hepatitis B infection, and an unexpected discovery about the composer’s family tree. According to University of Cambridge, one of the most famous locks, known as the Hiller Lock, was not from Beethoven but from a woman. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW See also Small chip implanted behind the eye connects to glasses with a camera, transforms images into visual stimuli, and can restore part of the vision lost due to macular degeneration. Without a car, an engineering student builds an electric wooden motorcycle from cedar parts equipped with a 2,000 W motor, hydraulic brakes, and lighting, and puts the vehicle to work on the streets. Arctic sea ice experiences the largest annual drop of the winter peak phase since the beginning of satellite measurements, losing 5.8% of its extent between 2024 and 2025, ending the apparent pause that concealed the ongoing reduction in a region crucial for the climate. Scientists discover a surprising “brain” hidden in the heart, formed by neurons capable of controlling the heartbeat and protecting the organ during stressful situations. The study analyzed eight locks attributed to Beethoven The research examined eight hair samples historically associated with Beethoven. The goal was to authenticate the material, sequence the composer’s genome, and search for clues about diseases that marked his life. According to the article published in Current Biology, five locks came from the same European man and were considered compatible with Beethoven’s documented origin. These samples allowed for a deeper genomic analysis. The best-preserved sample was the so-called Stumpff Lock. From it, scientists sequenced Beethoven’s nuclear genome with an average coverage of 24 times, a sufficient level to investigate ancestry, genetic risks, and signs of ancient pathogens. The most famous lock was not from Beethoven The biggest turnaround in the study involved the so-called Hiller Lock, a lock of hair traditionally associated with the composer and supposedly cut the day after his death. It had already been used in previous analyses that reinforced hypotheses about lead poisoning. CREDIT: KEVIN BROWN / AMERICAN BEETHOVEN SOCIETY The new sequencing showed that this lock did not belong to Beethoven. According to the University of Cambridge, the material came from a woman, not the German composer. This discovery weakens old conclusions based solely on this sample. As explained by the Beethoven-Haus Bonn, previous analyses done exclusively on the Hiller Lock can no longer be directly applied to Beethoven. Sequencing revealed genetic risk for liver disease The study found in Beethoven a relevant genetic predisposition for liver disease. The analysis identified variants associated with a higher risk of progressive liver problems. According to the University of Cambridge repository, Beethoven was homozygous for a variant in the PNPLA3 gene, strongly associated with progressive liver disease. news.title_zh: 贝多芬的头发经过基因测序,揭示了肝病、乙型肝炎的风险和一个家族秘密,但保存了近 200 年的最著名的头发之一甚至不是他的,而是属于一位女性。- CPG Click 石油和天然气
news.source_body_en: A recent genetic study of Ludwig van Beethoven's hair has uncovered new insights into his health and ancestry. Researchers analyzed eight locks attributed to the composer, with five samples confirmed as authentic through genetic compatibility. The sequencing revealed a genetic predisposition to liver disease and evidence of hepatitis B infection before his death in 1827. However, a significant discovery was that the famous Hiller Lock, long associated with Beethoven and used in previous studies, actually belonged to a woman. This finding invalidates earlier conclusions based solely on this sample. The study, published in Current Biology, highlights the importance of genetic authentication in historical research.

news.content: Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global EditionASIA 中文双语Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE China News Society Innovation HK/Macao Cross-Strait Cover Story Photo Environment Health Military Video Home / China / Society Home China Society Health campaign spotlights hepatitis B prevention across all ages chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-07-19 18:38 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE Runners are seen during a health campaign to control and eliminate hepatitis B in Beijing on Saturday. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] With four years remaining until the 2030 target for eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat domestically, public health officials and clinicians gathered in Beijing to assess progress and map out next steps in hepatitis B control. Hepatitis B remains a major public health challenge in China. An estimated 75 million people aged 1 to 69 are living with chronic HBV infection, accounting for roughly one-third of global cases. A significant proportion of those infected are unaware of their status. The virus is highly contagious, and chronic infection can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Since the introduction of universal free infant vaccination in 2005, coverage rates have climbed to 99.6% for the three-dose series and 95.6% for the timely birth dose—well above the global average of 85%. As a result, the prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen among children under five has dropped to 0.30%, down from much higher levels in the 1990s. Among the broader population aged 1 to 69, the prevalence now stands at 5.86%. These achievements do not mark the finish line. In September 2025, the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration and eight other government departments jointly issued an action plan for As part of the 2025–2030 action plan for addressing the disease, efforts to maintain high childhood vaccination rates while expanding adult immunization coverage are in full swing. Yao Fengli, deputy chief pediatrician at the Fifth Medical Center of the People's Liberation Army General Hospital, said that infants infected with HBV face a 90% risk of developing chronic infection, with long-term risks of cirrhosis and liver cancer. She urged that newborns should receive their first vaccine dose promptly after birth, followed by doses at one month and six months of age. As children enter preschool and school settings, group activities and close contact increase the risk of horizontal transmission. Parents should monitor their children's antibody levels and consult healthcare providers about screening and booster doses when necessary. Lyv Sa, senior physician at the Fifth Medical Center of the People's Liberation Army General Hospital’s liver disease department, said that HBV is not transmitted through everyday contact such as handshakes, hugging, shared meals, or attending classes together. She called for reducing stigma and encouraging family members of those infected to know their immune status and take appropriate preventive measures. Zhang Ying, chief physician at the Tianjin CDC, said that grassroots health centers play a critical role in delivering health education, on-site screening, vaccination reminders, and standardized follow-up care. The 2025-2030 action plan focuses on maintaining high childhood vaccination rates while expanding adult coverage, with grassroots health centers playing a key role in education and screening. Experts emphasize prompt newborn vaccination, antibody monitoring for children, and reducing stigma to encourage preventive measures among families.

news.content_title: Phase 3 results for hepatitis B treatment show functional cure for 1 in 5 people
news.content: Share on Pinterest Phase 3 trials suggest bepirovirsen can achieve a functional cure in about one in five people with hepatitis B. Image credit: Getty Images / Liliya Krueger In two phase 3 clinical trials, roughly one in five adults with chronic hepatitis B achieved sustained loss of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and undetectable hepatitis B viral DNA after completing a finite course of bepirovirsen treatment. Bepirovirsen reduces HBsAg production, aiming to restore the immune system’s ability to control the infection rather than simply suppressing viral replication. Participants with lower baseline HBsAg levels experienced higher functional cure rates, suggesting patient selection may play an important role in treatment success. While the results represent promising steps toward a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B, further research is necessary to improve response rates, evaluate long-term durability, and determine how the therapy performs in broader patient populations. Chronic hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver and remains a major global health challenge . Estimates suggest that roughly 250 million people are living with chronic hepatitis B, which predisposes them to develop severe complications, such as cirrhosis , liver failure , and liver cancer . Current first-line treatment will typically involve antiviral therapy to suppress viral replication. However, these drugs rarely eliminate hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), which is a key marker of persistent infection. Thus, many individuals may need to continue treatment indefinitely. As a result, researchers have increasingly focused on therapies capable of achieving a functional cure , defined as sustained loss of HBsAg and undetectable HBV DNA after treatment has ended. Now, results from two large phase 3 clinical trials indicate that the investigational drug bepirovirsen could mark a significant step toward a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B, offering hope beyond lifelong antiviral treatment for some patients. The findings, published in the New England Journal of Medicine , showed that approximately 20% of eligible patients achieved a sustained functional cure after completing a finite course of treatment, an outcome not observed in those receiving a placebo. What did the phase 3 trials find? The phase 3 B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 studies enrolled more than 1,800 adults with non-cirrhotic chronic hepatitis B across 29 countries, who had been receiving nucleotide analogue (NA) treatment for at least 6 months between 2022 and 2025. Participants were randomly assigned 2:1 to receive either 300 milligrams (mg) subcutaneous injections of bepirovirsen or a placebo weekly for 24 weeks, in addition to background NA therapy, followed by an additional 24 weeks of NA treatment. All participants had an HBsAg level of more than 100 to 3000 international units per milliliter (IU/ml). Eligible individuals discontinued NA therapy at 48 weeks. The primary outcome was a functional cure at week 72, defined as maintaining undetectable hepatitis B viral DNA and loss of HBsAg for at least 24 weeks after stopping treatment. After 72 weeks of follow-up, researchers found that: around 20% of patients receiving bepirovirsen achieved a functional cure no patients receiving placebo met the functional cure endpoint patients with lower baseline HBsAg levels appeared even more likely to respond, with functional cure rates reaching approximately 26% in some subgroups. Speaking to Medical News Today , study author Seng-Gee Lim , MD, Director of Hepatology at the National University Health System, Singapore, emphasized the importance of the trial findings: “Functional cure rate of 19% in Hepatitis B patients with HBsAg level [under] 3,000 IU/ml and 26% in those with HBsAg [under] 1,000 IU/ml. This finding provides meaningful cure rates for the first time for hepatitis B patients” “These findings are encouraging because they show researchers are making real progress towards treatments that go beyond simply controlling hepatitis B,” Opel Baker , MBChB, DipOccMed, MRCGP, general practitioner at the Mayfield Clinic Brighton and Hove, in the United Kinhdom, who was not involved in the study, explained to MNT . “While the treatment won’t work for everyone, every successful clinical trial helps us understand the disease better and brings us closer to more effective, personalised therapies. It’s an exciting step forward in a field that has seen relatively little therapeutic innovation for many years,” said Baker. Why are these results important? Bepirovirsen belongs to a class of medicines called antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) . Unlike existing antiviral therapies, which primarily block viral replication, antisense therapies target the virus’ messenger RNA. This reduces production of viral proteins, including HBsAg, which researchers believe may play an important role in suppressing the body’s immune response against the hepatitis B virus. Lowering HBsAg levels may allow the immune system to regain some of its ability to recognize and control infected liver cells. Earlier clinical studies demonstrated that bepirovirsen could substantially reduce HBsAg levels, although durable functional cures remained relatively uncommon. Experts have long considered a functional cure one of the most important goals in hepatitis B research. Researchers hoped larger phase 3 studies would determine whether these responses could be achieved more consistently. While current treatments can suppress viral replication, they rarely clear HBsAg. This means that people remain at risk of viral reactivation if treatment is stopped. These findings suggest that a finite treatment course could allow some individuals to discontinue therapy while maintaining viral control. “A functional cure would be a major breakthrough for people living with chronic hepatitis B,” Baker highlighted to MNT . “Although current antiviral treatments are very effective at suppressing the virus, they rarely remove the need for long-term monitoring or treatment. A functional cure could reduce the risk of serious complications such as cirrhosis and liver cancer, lessen the psychological burden of living with a chronic infection and improve patients’ quality of life.” – Opel Baker, MBChB, DipOccMed, MRCGP Similarly, Lim also highlighted the importance of achieving a functional cure on liver and psychological health. “Clinical studies and meta analyses show that loss of HBsAg as seen in functional cure is associated with even more benefits than just viral control with suppressing the virus — more significant reductions in liver cancer, liver failure and mortality,” the researcher told us. “Moreover, compliance with long term antiviral therapy is suboptimal, while functional cure means patients are off all therapy. Functional cure has also important patient related benefits such as loss of stigmatisation and improvement in psychological health,” he added. Further research still necessary While encouraging, the results do not represent a functional cure for all people living with chronic hepatitis B. The trials enrolled a specific group of patients, including those without cirrhosis and with relatively low HBsAg levels. As such, it remains unclear whether similar outcomes would be achieved in broader populations. Additionally, roughly four out of five participants did not achieve a functional cure, highlighting the continued need for improved therapies and combination treatment approaches. Bepirovirsen was also associated with more adverse events than placebo, although many were mild to moderate. Longer-term follow-up will also be necessary to determine how durable these responses remain over many years and whether a functional cure translates into lower rates of liver cancer and other complications. The researchers plan further investigations to determine whether combining bepirovirsen with immune-based treatments, including therapeutic vaccines and other novel agents, could further improve cure rates. Although additional research and regulatory review remain ahead, the latest results suggest a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B may be moving closer to routine clinical practice. “It’s important to remember that research is moving fast, and there is a genuine reason for optimism,” Baker noted. “Although these treatments are still being evaluated, advances like this offer hope that future therapies may provide better long-term outcomes. In the meantime, patients should continue taking any prescribed medication, attend regular monitoring appointments and speak to their healthcare team before making any changes to their treatment,” he added According to Lim, “bepirovirsen is the first step towards functional cure, and this is hope for those living with hepatitis B but better therapies will lead to higher cure rates in the future.”

news.content: Home Next What are the effects of Hepatitis B, and why should one vaccinate? Gastroenterologist Dr Ayush Dhingra explains Hepatitis B infects the liver and can cause chronic disorders in the organ over time. According to Dr Dhingra, vaccination is the best way to stay safe. Updated on: Jul 22, 2026, 18:31:13 IST By Debapriya Bhattacharya Prefer HT on Google Share via Copy link Hepatitis B is a viral infection that targets the liver, progressing silently before symptoms become noticeable. By the time many people realise something is wrong, liver damage has already taken place. Hepatitis B often evades early detection, shares Dr Ayush Dhingra. (Pexel) Also Read | Do mental workouts matter as much as physical exercise? Neurosurgeon Dr Anurag Saxena explains In an interaction with HT Lifestyle, Dr Ayush Dhingra reassured that Hepatitis B is one of the most preventable viral infections , making timely vaccination the smartest health decision a family can take. While our busy lifestyles can make it difficult to find time for vaccination, not taking the vaccine at all can come at a very high cost. What are the effects of Hepatitis B According to Dr Dhingra, there is yet to be widespread awareness about the effects of Hepatitis B. Unlike illnesses that announce their arrival with fever or cough, Hepatitis B quietly remains in the body for years. “Standard blood tests may appear normal even when the virus is causing underlying liver damage,” shared the gastroenterologist. “By the time symptoms like fatigue, jaundice, abdominal pain, or distension appear, the liver has already been damaged severely.” Some people naturally recover from the disease. However, those who do not develop a chronic infection are at increased risk of liver cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer. “Since infected people may not know they carry the virus, they unknowingly pass it on through infected blood, from mother to baby during childbirth or through unsafe exposure of body fluids,” noted Dr Dhingra. The importance of vaccination against Hepatitis B Vaccination is the best way to protect oneself from Hepatitis B. (Pexel) Dr Dhingra believes that prevention is the best defence against Hepatitis B. By delaying vaccination, a person leaves themselves vulnerable to an infection that has lifelong consequences like cirrhosis, liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) and other conditions like glomerulonephritis, dermatologic, and rheumatologic. “Advanced liver disease demands prolonged treatment and major lifestyle changes. In severe cases where the liver loses its ability to function, liver transplantation becomes the only life-saving treatment that helps to improve quality of life,” warned the gastroenterologist. Delaying Hepatitis B vaccination leaves individuals vulnerable to infection during the period they remain unprotected. This is particularly concerning for newborns, as babies infected during birth have a very high risk of developing chronic Hepatitis B, which can lead to lifelong liver damage. Similarly, adults who postpone vaccination due to lack of awareness or misconceptions may unknowingly remain at risk through routine medical procedures, occupational exposure, or close household contact with an infected person. “Since Hepatitis B often progresses silently without noticeable symptoms, many people are diagnosed only after significant liver damage has already occurred. Timely vaccination not only prevents infection but also reduces the long-term risk of cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer,” stated Dr Dhingra. Note to readers: This article is for informational purposes only and not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always seek the advice of your doctor with any questions about a medical condition. Dr Ayush Dhingra , MBBS, MD, DNB, is a consultant in the department of Gastroenterology at Manipal Hospital, Gurugram. news.content_title: Occult hepatitis B mutations drive liver cancer growth via Akt mTOR pathway
news.content: Occult hepatitis B virus (OBI) infection presents a significant global health challenge, notoriously flying under the radar of standard viral screening while relentlessly driving the pathogenesis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). A critical but poorly understood factor in OBI-related tumorigenesis is the frequent emergence of mutations in the HBV pre-S genomic region. While these mutations are known to correlate with advanced liver disease, the precise molecular mechanisms by which they hijack host cellular machinery to fuel unregulated tumor growth have remained largely elusive. This new research, published in Genes & Diseases by researchers from National Center of Gerontology, Beijing Engineering Research Center of Laboratory Medicine and Peking Union Medical College, investigated the oncogenic capacity of specific OBI-associated pre-S mutations to uncover their role in aberrant cell proliferation. Through rigorous in vitro molecular experiments utilizing constructed wild-type and mutated full-length HBV plasmids transfected into human hepatoma (Huh-7) cells, the researchers systematically evaluated cellular growth and cycle dynamics. The data revealed that specific OBI-associated pre-S mutations - namely E39K, D44N, N98T, H128R, and I161T - accelerate the G1/S phase transition of the cell cycle, leading to aggressive cellular proliferation. Comprehensive protein analyses deciphered the underlying intracellular networks, demonstrating that these mutations aggressively up-regulate the expression of the large hepatitis B surface protein (LHBs). This excessive LHBs subsequently triggers a massive activation of the Akt/mTOR signaling cascade, which strongly up-regulates the cell cycle driver Cyclin D1 and its associated kinases CDK4 and CDK6. This targeted protein surge dismantles normal cellular checkpoints, unleashing uncontrolled cell division. To directly counter these severe hyper-proliferative effects, the researchers explored the therapeutic potential of targeted kinase inhibitors. Remarkably, advanced cellular assays confirmed that administering the highly specific Akt inhibitor MK2206 or the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin successfully intercepted this malignant cascade, decisively suppressing the mutation -driven hyper-proliferation and arresting the cells back in the G0/G1 phase. By chemically blocking the Akt/mTOR signaling axis, these targeted therapies stripped the mutated hepatoma cells of their oncogenic growth advantage, fundamentally shielding the liver cells from unchecked replication. While these comprehensive data robustly highlight the critical influence of OBI-associated pre-S mutations in regulating the cell cycle, additional clinical studies are necessary to translate these targeted interventions into human therapies. In conclusion, elucidating the oncogenic role of the LHBs-Akt/mTOR/Cyclin D1 signaling network offers a powerful new strategy to combat OBI-related liver cancer. This significant finding directly positions specific Akt and mTOR inhibitors as highly compelling therapeutic candidates for the next generation of precision hepatocellular carcinoma treatments. Source: Journal reference: Sun, H., et al. (2025). Potential oncogenic role of occult hepatitis B virus pre-S mutations: Activation of Akt/mTOR/Cyclin D1 signaling drives cell cycle dysregulation and proliferation in hepatocellular carcinogenesis. Genes & Diseases. DOI: 10.1016/j.gendis.2025.101919. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352304225004088?via%3Dihub

news.source_body_en: A new study published in Genes & Diseases reveals how occult hepatitis B virus (OBI) pre-S mutations drive liver cancer growth by activating the Akt/mTOR signaling pathway. Researchers from National Center of Gerontology and Peking Union Medical College identified specific mutations (E39K, D44N, N98T, H128R, I161T) that accelerate cell cycle transition and proliferation in human hepatoma cells. These mutations up-regulate large hepatitis B surface protein (LHBs), triggering the Akt/mTOR cascade and increasing Cyclin D1 and associated kinases. news.content_zh: 发表在《基因与疾病》杂志上的一项新研究揭示了神秘的 乙型肝炎病毒 (OBI) pre-S 突变 如何通过激活 Akt/mTOR 信号通路来驱动肝癌生长。国家老年学中心和北京协和医学院的研究人员发现了加速人肝癌细胞细胞周期转变和增殖的特定突变(E39K、D44N、N98T、H128R、I161T)。这些 突变 上调大型乙型肝炎表面蛋白 (LHB),触发 Akt/mTOR 级联并增加 Cyclin D1 和相关激酶。值得注意的是,靶向激酶抑制剂 MK2206 和雷帕霉素成功抑制了这种过度增殖。虽然这些发现为精准肝细胞癌 治疗 提供了一种有前途的策略,但还需要进行更多的临床研究来将这些干预措施转化为人类疗法。

Bishkek time Time 02:23 USD 87.45 EUR 101.76 RUB 1.19 USD 87.45 EUR 101.76 RUB 1.19 KZT 0.18 UZS 0.01 Categories Search Find Categories Власть Общество Экономика Происшествия Агент 024 Спорт Техноблог Спецпроекты Кыргызча English Бизнес English 12:50, 23 July 2026, Bishkek - 24.kg news agency , by Myrzaiym ZHANYBEK KYZY More than 1,200 people registered with hepatitis B and C in Osh, Osh region 12:50, 23 July 2026, Bishkek - 24.kg news agency , by Myrzaiym ZHANYBEK KYZY A total of 1,204 people in Osh and Osh region are registered with viral hepatitis B and C, data from the Osh Regional Center for the Control of Blood-Borne Infections, Viral Hepatitis, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus say. During the first half of 2026, at least 785 people in Osh region and the city of Osh were registered with hepatitis B. Of them, 609 people live in Osh region, while 176 are residents of Osh city. news.content: Culture Economics Education In the world Sport Tourism Technologies Health Energy Society Transport WC-2026 Business Politics Culture Economics Education In the world Sport Tourism Technologies Health Energy Society Transport WC-2026 Business Politics Culture Economics Education In the world Sport Tourism Technologies Health All categories 18.03.2025 13371 Share on social network WHO strengthens medical professionals’ capacity in Turkmenistan on viral hepatitis B The World Health Organization (WHO) Country Office in Turkmenistan held a training course on the "Diagnostics and treatment of viral hepatitis B according to WHO recommendations and national protocol" from March 12 to 13, 2025. The course led by WHO/Europe consultant, Professor Alexander Nersesov, aims to enhance the capacity of Turkmen medical professionals in their effort to combat viral hepatitis B. The skill-building session was conducted at the Infectious disease treatment-prevention center in videoconference mode. The participants of the event were doctors specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of viral hepatitis from the Infectious disease treatment-prevention center of the Directorate of Infectious Diseases Centers, primary health care providers, infectious diseases specialists from the institutions at the district level, and representatives from the department of infectious diseases at the State Medical University named after Myrat Karryev. The training covered essential information on hepatitis B, its diagnosis, classification, and treatment, with specific guidance for chronic cases, pregnancy, and special patient groups, as well as hepatitis D. This training is designed to equip medical professionals with the updated knowledge and best practices in viral hepatitis B diagnosis and treatment, aligning with both WHO guidelines and national protocols. By enhancing the skills of healthcare providers, this initiative will contribute to improved patient outcomes and strengthen Turkmenistan's efforts to control and manage viral hepatitis. We have a range of modules and videos ranging from 2 minutes up to 15 minutes. There is something for everyone, even if you are short on time. Can I save content for later? Yes. If you see a piece of learning you would like to take, but haven’t got time right now, you can “Bookmark” it for later. Please note you need to have a registered account and be logged in to access this feature. Can I record my learning outcomes? Yes, logged in members can record their learning outcomes on any piece of content and save them in their learning log. Pharmacists and technicians can do this using recording templates in line with GPhC requirements. How do I get a learning log? You have to register an account on Pharmacy Magazine and login to access your personal, secure learning log. What does my learning log do? It documents all the learning you have recorded, including completed learning, learning in progress and bookmarked learning you have saved to do later. If I’m a pharmacist or pharmacy technician, can the log help me fulfil the GPhC’s revalidation requirements? Yes, pharmacists and pharmacy technicians also have the ability to record and add their own revalidation entries to their learning log in line with GPhC requirements. If I’m a member of more than one website on The Pharmacy Magazine, can I access all my learning in my learning log even if I’ve recorded it on different websites? Yes, if you record learning on more than one website, it will be displayed in your learning log which is shared across all the accounts you have registered with The Pharmacy Magazine. How do I view/print a certificate of my learning? Certificates are available at the end of every module, after the assessment questions. They are also accessible via the learning log. How do I change my personal details, email address and password? Login and click on “Settings” in your member menu and click on the relevant links to change any of your details. All saved changes take immediate effect. If I leave the industry and want to delete my account, can I do so? Yes absolutely. You are able to delete your account at any time but please be aware that by doing so you will also delete any historical learning records you have in your learning log. If I have a query or I’m stuck, how can I get help? You will need to have registered an account to get help. Logged in members can click on the “Helpdesk” link in their Settings and submit a Helpdesk ticket. We endeavour to respond to new Helpdesk tickets within 24 hours during office hours (9pm to 5pm Mon to Fri) How can I check on your Terms of Service, Privacy Policy and Cookie Policy? You can click on the relevant links in the footer of the website. If there are any proposed changes to any of our Policies, we will email registered members in advance. Is Pharmacy Magazine GDPR compliant? Yes we are and we take your privacy and the security of your data extremely seriously. Please read the Privacy Policy for further details. Logged in members can click on the “My data” link in “Settings” to download a copy of all the personal data we currently hold on you. Who is the company that owns and operates Pharmacy Magazine? Communications International Group Limited (CIG), the largest, most experienced publisher in the UK pharmacy sector. CIG is one of the UK’s leading provider of sector-specific news and training, publishing 15 healthcare and beauty titles including Pharmacy Magazine, Training Matters, P3Pharmacy, Independent Community Pharmacist and Beauty Magazine. Over the years the company has built an enviable reputation in pharmacy, journalism, education, training, regulatory, awards and conferences, that today amounts to more than 350 years of healthcare industry experience. Visit Helpdesk You recently searched for Popular Searches You recently searched for Popular Searches National monitoring and prescribing guidance on hepatitis B reactivation is lacking Neil Trainis, 21 Jul 20262 Min National monitoring and prescribing guidance on hepatitis B reactivation is lacking Neil Trainis, 21 Jul 20262 Min In News Follow this topic Bookmark Record learning outcomes A coroner in North London has called for more national guidance on which services should be responsible for monitoring and prescribing medication to prevent hepatitis B becoming active again after the death of a patient whose treatment was inadvertently discontinued. Tung Thanh Tran, 41, died at the Royal Free Hospital in September 2025 after being diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B following a renal transplant in 2013. An inquest into his death heard he was discharged from hepatology but continued to receive the viral reactivation prophylaxis entecavir from renal transplant services. By the start of 2025, the medication was being delivered to his home but was then “inadvertently discontinued as there was a presumption that hepatology would continue to prescribe” it. In his report, sent to the British Association for the Study of the Liver (BASL) and the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the coroner for Inner North London Richard Brittain said Tran appeared “to have understood this to have been an intentional change of his medication”. Tran was admitted to his local hospital in August 2025 with signs of acute liver disease from reactivation of hepatitis B and transferred to the Royal Free Hospital, where he died on September 12, 2025. “He was too unwell to be considered for liver transplant,” Brittain noted in his report. He recorded the cause of death as acute liver failure, sepsis (unknown source), hepatitis B reactivation owing to cessation of medication and immunosuppression for renal transplantation. “Mr Tran died of complications arising from reactivation of a viral illness, which arose from inadvertent discontinuation of necessary medical treatment,” the report concluded. Brittain told BASL that Tran’s death gave rise to concerns about “a lack of national guidance regarding which services should be responsible for the monitoring and prescribing in relation to hepatitis B reactivation prevention”. Brittain also told the UKHSA: “There is a large population of patients who are found to have hepatitis B infection through opt-out screening in emergency departments but there is a lack of specialised commissioning to maintain subsequent engagement with services. “I heard that this differs from the position with regards to hepatitis C and HIV services, even though these patient populations are smaller.” The report was also sent to Tran’s family and the Royal Free Hospital. _ https://www.pharmacymagazine.co.uk/news/national-monitoring-and-prescribing-guidance-on-hepatitis-b-reactivation-is-lacking Copy Link Record my learning outcomes Save for later News Clinical #Hepatitis #Liver #Prescription medicines #Coroner Share: In News Stay up to date with all the news, learning and insight in the world of pharmacy. Visit Helpdesk You recently searched for Popular Searches You recently searched for Popular Searches National monitoring and prescribing guidance on hepatitis B reactivation is lacking Neil Trainis, 21 Jul 20262 Min National monitoring and prescribing guidance on hepatitis B reactivation is lacking Neil Trainis, 21 Jul 20262 Min In News Follow this topic Bookmark Record learning outcomes A coroner in North London has called for more national guidance on which services should be responsible for monitoring and prescribing medication to prevent hepatitis B becoming active again after the death of a patient whose treatment was inadvertently discontinued. Tung Thanh Tran, 41, died at the Royal Free Hospital in September 2025 after being diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B following a renal transplant in 2013. An inquest into his death heard he was discharged from hepatology but continued to receive the viral reactivation prophylaxis entecavir from renal transplant services. By the start of 2025, the medication was being delivered to his home but was then “inadvertently discontinued as there was a presumption that hepatology would continue to prescribe” it. In his report, sent to the British Association for the Study of the Liver (BASL) and the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the coroner for Inner North London Richard Brittain said Tran appeared “to have understood this to have been an intentional change of his medication”. Tran was admitted to his local hospital in August 2025 with signs of acute liver disease from reactivation of hepatitis B and transferred to the Royal Free Hospital, where he died on September 12, 2025. “He was too unwell to be considered for liver transplant,” Brittain noted in his report. He recorded the cause of death as acute liver failure, sepsis (unknown source), hepatitis B reactivation owing to cessation of medication and immunosuppression for renal transplantation. “Mr Tran died of complications arising from reactivation of a viral illness, which arose from inadvertent discontinuation of necessary medical treatment,” the report concluded. Brittain told BASL that Tran’s death gave rise to concerns about “a lack of national guidance regarding which services should be responsible for the monitoring and prescribing in relation to hepatitis B reactivation prevention”. Brittain also told the UKHSA: “There is a large population of patients who are found to have hepatitis B infection through opt-out screening in emergency departments but there is a lack of specialised commissioning to maintain subsequent engagement with services. “I heard that this differs from the position with regards to hepatitis C and HIV services, even though these patient populations are smaller.” The report was also sent to Tran’s family and the Royal Free Hospital. _ https://www.pharmacymagazine.co.uk/news/national-monitoring-and-prescribing-guidance-on-hepatitis-b-reactivation-is-lacking Copy Link Record my learning outcomes Save for later News Clinical #Hepatitis #Liver #Prescription medicines #Coroner Share: In News Stay up to date with all the news, learning and insight in the world of pharmacy. news.content: A coroner’s report published after a patient died of complications from a hepatitis B reactivation warned that there is “significant risk of future deaths”. A “lack of national guidance” on monitoring and prescribing for hepatitis B reactivation poses a “significant risk of future deaths”, a coroner has warned. In a prevention of future deaths report published earlier this month, assistant coroner for Inner London North Richard Brittain noted that Tung Tran, 41, died in September 2025 of complications from a hepatitis B reactivation caused by “inadvertent discontinuation of necessary medical treatment”. The report said Tran was diagnosed with hepatitis B after a renal transplant in 2013 and, “after a period of disengagement from services”, was “discharged from hepatology but continued to receive viral reactivation prophylaxis, Entecavir, from renal transplant services”. It added that Tran’s medication supply changed to home delivery in early 2025, but Entecavir was “inadvertently discontinued”, with the “presumption that hepatology would continue to prescribe this”. Tran “appears to have understood this to have been an intentional change of his medication”, Brittain said. Read more: Coroner warns of prescribing errors after prison death “He attended his local hospital in August 2025 with signs of acute liver disease from reactivation of hepatitis B and was transferred to the Royal Free Hospital,” he added. “He was too unwell to be considered for liver transplant and sadly died on September 12, 2025′′. According to the report, an inquest into Tran’s death found the medical cause to be acute liver failure, sepsis, hepatitis B reactivation “owing to cessation of medication” and immunosuppression for renal transplantation. Brittain highlighted to the British Viral Hepatitis group at the British Association for the Study of the Liver (BASL) a concern that “there is a lack of national guidance regarding which services should be responsible for monitoring and prescribing in relation to hepatitis B reactivation prevention”. He also directed a concern to the UK Health Security Agency, noting that although a “large population” of patients are found to have hepatitis B through opt-out screenings at emergency departments, “there is a lack of specialised commissioning to maintain subsequent engagement with services”. And he said that “unless action is taken to address” the concerns, there is “a significant risk of future deaths”. Read more: ‘Highly toxic’: Coroner warns GPs of propranolol overdose risk In its response, the BASL said it “does not lead the development or publication of clinical guidelines”. It added that there “is variation between NHS Trusts” as to whether monitoring and prescribing for patients at risk of hepatitis B reactivation in the setting of immunosuppressive treatment is “delivered by the treating team or whether specialist hepatology services are involved”. “We have previously and will again incorporate the risks of hepatitis B reactivation and its prevention and management into our webinar and conference programmes in this coming year,” it said. Read more: Coroner warns of issues with epilepsy meds availability It comes after a coroner raised concerns earlier this year over prescribing errors at HMP Thameside following the death of an inmate. And it follows a coroner warning GPs of the risk of propranolol overdose after the death of a man who took a “significant amount” of the drug. Declan joined C+D as a reporter in July 2026. He has previous bylines in The Drinks Business magazine and graduated with an MA in Journalism from City St George's, University of London with Distinction earlier this year. The regulator has updated product information for the drug to include a contraindication for patients with phaeochromocytoma. The analysis also revealed that 67% of Pharmacy First users were female and 59% were aged below 40. analysis.brief_en: A coroner has called for improved national guidance on hepatitis B reactivation prescribing after a patient died following the inadvertent discontinuation of necessary medication. Tung Tran, 41, died in September 2025 from complications of hepatitis B reactivation caused by the cessation of Entecavir, which he had been receiving since a 2013 renal transplant. The coroner directed concerns to the British Viral Hepatitis group and the UK Health Security Agency, noting variation in NHS practices and gaps in specialized commissioning for hepatitis B patients identified through emergency screenings. The British Association for the Study of the Liver acknowledged the issue but stated it does not develop clinical guidelines, instead planning to incorporate the risks into educational programs.

Newswise — Each year, millions of people live with chronic hepatitis B that slowly develops into cirrhosis. Once cirrhosis patients suffer decompensation issues including fluid buildup in the belly and dangerous esophageal bleeding, their risks of repeated hospital stays and early death rise sharply.Clinicians mostly judge liver risk through one-time liver blood tests, which miss gradual whole-body tissue changes that drive disease deterioration. In a study published in Hepatobiliary Communications, researchers from The First Hospital of Lanzhou University uncovered clear, stage-specific tissue patterns from standard CT scans to predict upcoming severe liver complications.“We found that visceral fat and muscle shifts carry totally different warning meaning based on how advanced a patient’s cirrhosis is,” shares co-lead author Xiaoyue Zhang. “For patients with compensated early-stage cirrhosis, gradual degeneration of visceral fat signals a significantly higher risk of complications, and for those who have already experienced severe hepatic decompensation events, persistent muscle wasting serves as the primary warning marker.”The researchers confirmed tracking long-term tissue shifts delivers much more accurate risk alerts than isolated examinations. “Above all, these fat and muscle changes can be spotted on routine abdominal CT scans that every cirrhosis patient already undergoes, with no extra expensive or invasive testing needed,” adds Zhang.According to senior and corresponding author Junfeng Li, the team’s findings addressed an unmet clinical demand in daily liver disease management. “Past research rarely split cirrhosis patients by disease stage to sort out these tissue warning signals,” explains Li. “This easy CT monitoring method allows clinicians to launch personalized nutritional and metabolic support early, effectively slowing liver damage and lifting long-term survival chances for hepatitis B cirrhosis patients.”###ReferencesDOI10.1016/j.hbc.2026.100003Original Source URLhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.hbc.2026.100003Funding InformationThis work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant no. 82360132]; analysis.brief_en: A new study from Chinese researchers, published in Hepatobiliary Communications, reveals that CT-measured changes in fat and muscle can predict severe liver complications in chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis patients. The study found that for patients with early-stage cirrhosis, gradual visceral fat degeneration signals higher complication risks, while for those with severe decompensation events, muscle wasting is the primary warning marker. These tissue patterns can be detected on routine abdominal CT scans, allowing clinicians to provide early personalized nutritional and metabolic support, potentially slowing liver damage and improving long-term survival. The research addresses a critical gap in current clinical practices that rely on one-time liver blood tests, which miss gradual whole-body tissue changes driving disease deterioration.

news.source_body_en: A new study from Chinese researchers, published in Hepatobiliary Communications, reveals that CT-measured changes in fat and muscle can predict severe liver complications in chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis patients. The study found that for patients with early-stage cirrhosis, gradual visceral fat degeneration signals higher complication risks, while for those with severe decompensation events, muscle wasting is the primary warning marker. These tissue patterns can be detected on routine abdominal CT scans, allowing clinicians to provide early personalized nutritional and metabolic support, potentially slowing liver damage and improving long-term survival. The research addresses a critical gap in current clinical practices that rely on one-time liver blood tests, which miss gradual whole-body tissue changes driving disease deterioration.
news.content_zh: 中国研究人员发表在《肝胆通讯》上的一项新研究表明,CT 测量的脂肪和肌肉变化可以预测 慢性乙型肝炎 相关肝硬化患者的严重肝脏并发症。研究发现,对于早期肝硬化患者来说,内脏脂肪逐渐退化预示着更高的并发症风险,而对于那些患有严重失代偿事件的患者来说,肌肉萎缩是主要的警告标志。这些组织模式可以通过常规腹部 CT 扫描检测到,使临床医生能够提供早期个性化的营养和代谢支持,有可能减缓肝损伤并提高长期生存率。该研究解决了目前依赖一次性肝脏血液测试的临床实践中的一个关键差距,这种测试错过了导致疾病恶化的逐渐的全身组织变化。

analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 调查:在同行评审期刊上发表的已完成研究。测试:使用常规腹部 CT 扫描,无需额外测试。预防:允许临床医生尽早启动个性化的营养和代谢支持。现状:研究结果解决了日常肝病管理中未满足的临床需求。不确定性:所提供的证据中未报告。

Tennessee man dead after Scott County car crash News |Region |EducationETSU researcher seeks cure for Hepatitis BFrom staff reportsPublished: Jul 20, 2026 2:01 PMUpdated: Jul 21, 2026 5:08 PMFeatured MediaPhoto Credit: CONTRIBUTEDDr. Zhi Q. YaoDr. Zhi Q. YaoCONTRIBUTED568317East Tennessee State University’s Dr. Zhi Q. Yao is leading the nation’s only National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded R33 project to advance to a second phase of research aimed at developing a cure for Hepatitis B.Yao, a professor in the Quillen College of Medicine’s Department of Internal Medicine, received the $1.76 million grant from the NIH’s Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) to continue developing a gene therapy approach that could eliminate the Hepatitis B infection, according to a press release from ETSU.The Phase II (R33) award follows the Phase 1 (R21) award Yao received in 2024 from the NIAID. Of the five research teams that received Phase I grants in 2024, Yao was the only one to receive Phase II funding.“This recognition reflects the progress our team has made toward developing a potential curative strategy for Hepatitis B,” Yao said. “The Phase II award allows us to build upon our earlier work with new gene-editing approaches that could ultimately eliminate the virus from infected cells.”Yao’s work focuses on improving the delivery of CRISPR-based gene editing technology. This research has led to the development of an exosome-based delivery system designed to target infected cells in the liver. Exosomes are small, cell-derived, membrane-bound structures that facilitate communication between cells by carrying proteins, lipids, RNA and other molecules.If successful, the approach could lead to therapies that eliminate the virus from the body rather than simply controlling it.“Being the only team selected to continue this work is an extraordinary accomplishment for Dr. Yao and his team,” Dr. Bill Block, Quillen’s dean and ETSU’s vice president for Clinical Affairs, said. “His award is not just a testament to his excellence as a researcher – it also speaks to the strength of our college’s research program, and our ability to impact health both inside and outside of a clinical setting.”The award reflects ETSU's growing research enterprise and its commitment to improving health through scientific discovery – advancing innovations that have the potential to benefit patients in Appalachia and beyond, according to the release. It also brings Yao’s total NIH funding in this line of research to more than $4.3 million.Yao serves as Quillen’s Paul Dishner Chair of Excellence, director of the college’s Center of Excellence for HIV/AIDS, and chief of the Department of Internal Medicine’s research division. Yao is also a member of ETSU’s Center of Excellence in Inflammation, Infectious Disease and Immunity. More information about the Quillen College of Medicine is available online at etsu.edu/com/. Tennessee man dead after Scott County car crash News |Region |EducationETSU researcher seeks cure for Hepatitis BFrom staff reportsPublished: Jul 20, 2026 2:01 PMUpdated: Jul 21, 2026 5:08 PMFeatured MediaPhoto Credit: CONTRIBUTEDDr. Zhi Q. YaoDr. Zhi Q. YaoCONTRIBUTED568317East Tennessee State University’s Dr. Zhi Q. Yao is leading the nation’s only National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded R33 project to advance to a second phase of research aimed at developing a cure for Hepatitis B.Yao, a professor in the Quillen College of Medicine’s Department of Internal Medicine, received the $1.76 million grant from the NIH’s Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) to continue developing a gene therapy approach that could eliminate the Hepatitis B infection, according to a press release from ETSU.The Phase II (R33) award follows the Phase 1 (R21) award Yao received in 2024 from the NIAID. Of the five research teams that received Phase I grants in 2024, Yao was the only one to receive Phase II funding.“This recognition reflects the progress our team has made toward developing a potential curative strategy for Hepatitis B,” Yao said. “The Phase II award allows us to build upon our earlier work with new gene-editing approaches that could ultimately eliminate the virus from infected cells.”Yao’s work focuses on improving the delivery of CRISPR-based gene editing technology. This research has led to the development of an exosome-based delivery system designed to target infected cells in the liver. Exosomes are small, cell-derived, membrane-bound structures that facilitate communication between cells by carrying proteins, lipids, RNA and other molecules.If successful, the approach could lead to therapies that eliminate the virus from the body rather than simply controlling it.“Being the only team selected to continue this work is an extraordinary accomplishment for Dr. Yao and his team,” Dr. Bill Block, Quillen’s dean and ETSU’s vice president for Clinical Affairs, said. “His award is not just a testament to his excellence as a researcher – it also speaks to the strength of our college’s research program, and our ability to impact health both inside and outside of a clinical setting.”The award reflects ETSU's growing research enterprise and its commitment to improving health through scientific discovery – advancing innovations that have the potential to benefit patients in Appalachia and beyond, according to the release. It also brings Yao’s total NIH funding in this line of research to more than $4.3 million.Yao serves as Quillen’s Paul Dishner Chair of Excellence, director of the college’s Center of Excellence for HIV/AIDS, and chief of the Department of Internal Medicine’s research division. Yao is also a member of ETSU’s Center of Excellence in Inflammation, Infectious Disease and Immunity. More information about the Quillen College of Medicine is available online at etsu.edu/com/. news.content_title: 90m Africans living with hepatitis B, C undiagnosed – Mahama
news.content: President John Dramani Mahama has expressed concern over the growing burden of diseases across Africa, saying they continue to claim lives and undermine the continent’s development. He said more than 90 million Africans living with hepatitis B or C remain undiagnosed, while malaria continues to pose a major health challenge. He also noted that non-communicable diseases account for more than two million deaths among Africans below the age of 70 each year. President Mahama made the remarks at the African Union Extraordinary Health Summit, where African Heads of State and Governments gathered to adopt a fully costed continental roadmap aimed at ending AIDS and tuberculosis by 2030. In his opening address, the President called on African leaders to intensify efforts to address the continent’s health challenges, stressing that Africa must move beyond traditional approaches to healthcare and pursue transformative solutions. “Neglected tropical diseases still blind, disfigure and stigmatise our people, and if you are observant you will notice that most accounts of the global infectious diseases burden present a uniquely depressing African perspective. “Africa now stands at a crossroad defined by its appetites for total health transformation. It can no longer allow itself to be purged on the periphery and cast as the destitute beneficiary of the largesse of some distant global health systems,” he said. President Mahama further urged leaders to ensure that commitments made at the summit translate into concrete actions and measurable outcomes rather than remain mere declarations. He said sustained political commitment, investment, and stronger health systems are essential to achieving lasting improvements in healthcare delivery across the continent. CT-measured fat and muscle changes predict severe liver complications in Chronic Hepatitis B-Related Cirrhosis Distributed by EIN Presswire FAYETTEVILLE, GA, UNITED STATES, July 20, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Researchers tracked longitudinal alterations in adipose and muscle tissue through routine CT scans. Worsening visceral fat tissue degeneration predicts complications for compensated chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis, while sustained muscle loss signals risk in decompensated patients. Each year, millions of people live with chronic hepatitis B that slowly develops into cirrhosis. Once cirrhosis patients suffer decompensation issues including fluid buildup in the belly and dangerous esophageal bleeding, their risks of repeated hospital stays and early death rise sharply. Clinicians mostly judge liver risk through one-time liver blood tests, which miss gradual whole-body tissue changes that drive disease deterioration. In a study published in Hepatobiliary Communications, researchers from The First Hospital of Lanzhou University uncovered clear, stage-specific tissue patterns from standard CT scans to predict upcoming severe liver complications. “We found that visceral fat and muscle shifts carry totally different warning meaning based on how advanced a patient’s cirrhosis is,” shares co-lead author Xiaoyue Zhang. “For patients with compensated early-stage cirrhosis, gradual degeneration of visceral fat signals a significantly higher risk of complications, and for those who have already experienced severe hepatic decompensation events, persistent muscle wasting serves as the primary warning marker.” The researchers confirmed tracking long-term tissue shifts delivers much more accurate risk alerts than isolated examinations. “Above all, these fat and muscle changes can be spotted on routine abdominal CT scans that every cirrhosis patient already undergoes, with no extra expensive or invasive testing needed,” adds Zhang. According to senior and corresponding author Junfeng Li, the team’s findings addressed an unmet clinical demand in daily liver disease management. “Past research rarely split cirrhosis patients by disease stage to sort out these tissue warning signals,” explains Li. “This easy CT monitoring method allows clinicians to launch personalized nutritional and metabolic support early, effectively slowing liver damage and lifting long-term survival chances for hepatitis B cirrhosis patients.” ReferencesDOI10.1016/j.hbc.2026.100003 Original Source URLhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.hbc.2026.100003 Funding InformationThis work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant no. 82360132]; the National College Students Innovation and Entrepreneurship Training Program [Grant no. 20250000009]; the Gansu Province College Students Innovation and Entrepreneurship Training Plan Project [Grant no. 20250060289]; the Excellence Program of Lanzhou University [Grant no. 20240060001]; the Lanzhou University College Students Innovation and Entrepreneurship [Grant nos. 20250020069, 20250020072]; the Gansu Province Joint Research Fund Project [Grant nos. 23JRRA1489, 24JRRA911]; and the Major Project of Scientific and Technological Innovation in the Health Industry of Gansu Province [Grant no. analysis.time: Published on July 20, 2026. Event date not explicitly reported in the evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Research conducted at The First Hospital of Lanzhou University. Study population includes patients with chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis.
analysis.event: Researchers identified that CT-measured fat and muscle changes can predict severe liver complications in chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis. The study found stage-specific tissue patterns: worsening visceral fat degeneration predicts complications in compensated early-stage patients, while sustained muscle loss signals risk in decompensated patients.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study addresses an unmet clinical need in liver disease management. Millions of people live with chronic hepatitis B that develops into cirrhosis. Decompensated patients face increased risks of repeated hospital stays and early death. The findings allow for early personalized nutritional and metabolic support to slow liver damage and improve long-term survival.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The research was published in Hepatobiliary Communications and supported by multiple funding sources. The method uses routine abdominal CT scans already performed on cirrhosis patients, requiring no additional testing. The findings provide a non-invasive way to monitor disease progression and guide clinical interventions.

analysis.brief_en: A groundbreaking study from The First Hospital of Lanzhou University reveals that routine CT scans can predict severe liver complications in chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis patients. Researchers discovered distinct tissue patterns: worsening visceral fat signals risk in early-stage compensated patients, while persistent muscle loss warns of danger in those with decompensated disease. This non-invasive monitoring method allows clinicians to intervene early with personalized nutritional support, potentially slowing liver damage and improving survival rates. The study addresses a critical gap in current clinical practice, which relies on one-time blood tests that miss gradual tissue changes driving disease progression. With millions living with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis globally, this approach offers a practical, cost-effective tool for better disease management.

analysis_en.location_and_population: Research conducted at The First Hospital of Lanzhou University. Study population includes patients with chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis.
analysis_en.event: Researchers identified that CT-measured fat and muscle changes can predict severe liver complications in chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis. The study found stage-specific tissue patterns: worsening visceral fat degeneration predicts complications in compensated early-stage patients, while sustained muscle loss signals risk in decompensated patients.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The study addresses an unmet clinical need in liver disease management. Millions of people live with chronic hepatitis B that develops into cirrhosis. Decompensated patients face increased risks of repeated hospital stays and early death. The findings allow for early personalized nutritional and metabolic support to slow liver damage and improve long-term survival.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The research was published in Hepatobiliary Communications and supported by multiple funding sources. The method uses routine abdominal CT scans already performed on cirrhosis patients, requiring no additional testing. The findings provide a non-invasive way to monitor disease progression and guide clinical interventions.

news.source_body_en: A groundbreaking study from The First Hospital of Lanzhou University reveals that routine CT scans can predict severe liver complications in chronic hepatitis B-related cirrhosis patients. Researchers discovered distinct tissue patterns: worsening visceral fat signals risk in early-stage compensated patients, while persistent muscle loss warns of danger in those with decompensated disease. This non-invasive monitoring method allows clinicians to intervene early with personalized nutritional support, potentially slowing liver damage and improving survival rates. The study addresses a critical gap in current clinical practice, which relies on one-time blood tests that miss gradual tissue changes driving disease progression. With millions living with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis globally, this approach offers a practical, cost-effective tool for better disease management.

news.content_title: Hepatitis Prevention Programs Improve Liver Outcomes, but Gaps in Screening, Care Remain
news.content: Hepatitis B and C virus (HBV/HCV) prevention programs incorporating screening, vaccination, early treatment, and long-term monitoring can improve detection, treatment uptake, and liver-related outcomes, according to a systematic review recently published in Public Health . 1 Assessing the Impact of HBV/HCV Prevention Programs Chronic HBV and HCV infections remain leading causes of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and long-term liver disease, highlighting the need for prevention strategies that extend beyond infection control. 2 Although advances such as direct-acting antivirals have transformed HCV treatment and expanded prevention efforts, gaps remain in identifying undiagnosed infections, ensuring timely treatment, and maintaining long-term liver disease monitoring. 1 In high-income countries, hepatitis prevention programs often focus on populations at increased risk, including people who inject drugs, individuals from hepatitis-endemic regions, and those facing socioeconomic barriers to care . This systematic review evaluated the effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and implementation challenges of HBV/HCV prevention programs aimed at addressing chronic liver disease and HCC through screening, vaccination, antiviral treatment, and ongoing surveillance. Researchers searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and Scopus for studies published between January 2013 and November 2025 evaluating HBV and/or HCV prevention programs in high-income countries. Included studies assessed strategies such as population-based screening, targeted outreach, vaccination, antiviral treatment, liver monitoring, and HCC surveillance. Early Treatment Associated With Lower HCC Risk and Reduced Costs Across 23 studies, community-based screening initiatives targeting populations at elevated risk identified undiagnosed HBV/HCV infections in 15.3% to 34.3% of screened individuals. In addition, integrated care pathways and monitoring programs enabled detection of advanced fibrosis in 5.3% to 46.2% of participants and HCC in 3.5% to 39.2%. Several successful programs used multidisciplinary models that combined primary care, specialty care, community organizations, and case management. These programs frequently incorporated point-of-care testing, noninvasive liver assessments, vaccination, antiviral therapy, and patient navigation services to improve linkage to care. The review also found that earlier diagnosis and treatment were associated with improved long-term liver outcomes. One population-based analysis included in the review found that individuals with cirrhosis had a 2.74-fold higher risk of developing HCC (adjusted sub-distribution HR [aSHR], 2.74; 95% CI, 1.78-4.22), whereas individuals who achieved sustained virologic response following HCV treatment experienced an 82% reduction in HCC risk (aSHR, 0.18; 95% CI, 0.12-0.27). Modeling studies also demonstrated potential population-level benefits from expanded prevention strategies. In Australia, expanded screening, access to antiviral treatment, and monitoring between 2015 and 2022 were estimated to prevent 969 HCV-related HCC cases and 1427 HCV-related deaths. Economic analyses consistently supported the value of prevention programs. Expanded HBV/HCV screening, early antiviral treatment, vaccination, and HCC surveillance were generally considered cost-effective, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios ranging from $1890 to $187,000 per quality-adjusted life-year gained. Implementation Barriers Continue to Affect Hepatitis Prevention Despite evidence supporting prevention strategies, several barriers limited program effectiveness. The review identified fragmented health care delivery, limited workforce capacity, inadequate harm-reduction services, unstable funding, incomplete patient data systems, and competing clinical priorities as challenges to implementation. Patient-level barriers also affected treatment initiation and long-term monitoring. The researchers noted that limited hepatitis awareness, stigma, socioeconomic instability, and difficulties maintaining follow-up contributed to gaps in care; across studies reporting these outcomes, loss to follow-up ranged from 11.5% to 39.6%. Programs demonstrating greater success incorporated accessible and subsidized testing and treatment, coordinated care pathways, automated health record reminders, and partnerships between health systems and community organizations. Integrated Care Models May Improve Long-Term Hepatitis Outcomes Based on their review, the authors concluded that hepatitis prevention efforts must extend beyond identifying infections by incorporating comprehensive care models spanning diagnosis, treatment, and surveillance. However, they acknowledged several limitations, including that most analyzed studies had limited follow-up periods and heterogeneous contexts and outcome measures, making long-term program effects unclear and reducing generalizability. The researchers emphasized that additional longitudinal research is needed to determine whether large-scale implementation of hepatitis prevention programs directly reduces HCC incidence and mortality. “...much of the evidence is constrained by small-scale implementation, inconsistent reporting, and limited examination of behavioural and structural determinants of participation and adherence,” they wrote. “Strengthening the implementation of patient-centered, integrated system-wide approaches is needed to support sustainable and equitable prevention efforts.” References Cai S, Dharmayani PNA, Lewandowska M, et al. Impacts of hepatitis B and C prevention programmes on long-term outcomes of advanced liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review. Public Health . Published online July 3, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.puhe.2026.106384 Llovet JM, Kelley RK, Villanueva A, et al. Hepatocellular carcinoma. Nat Rev Dis Primers . 2021;7(1):6. doi:10.1038/s41572-020-00240-3

analysis.brief_en: A systematic review published in Public Health demonstrates that hepatitis B and C virus prevention programs incorporating screening, vaccination, early treatment, and long-term monitoring significantly improve liver-related outcomes in high-income countries. Community-based screening identified undiagnosed infections in 15.3-34.3% of at-risk individuals, while integrated care detected advanced liver disease in 5.3-46.2% of participants. Earlier treatment was associated with reduced hepatocellular carcinoma risk, with Australia's expanded prevention efforts estimated to prevent 969 HCC cases and 1,427 deaths between 2015-2022. Despite these benefits, implementation challenges including fragmented healthcare, limited resources, and patient barriers like stigma and follow-up difficulties (11.5-39.6% loss to follow-up) continue to hinder program effectiveness. The authors emphasize the need for integrated, patient-centered approaches to achieve sustainable and equitable hepatitis prevention.

elements_zh.location_and_population: 高收入国家,重点关注高风险人群,包括注射吸毒者、来自肝炎流行地区的个人以及面临护理方面的社会经济障碍的人。
elements_zh.event: 《公共卫生》杂志上发表的一项系统综述发现,结合筛查、疫苗接种、早期 治疗 和长期监测的乙型和丙型肝炎病毒 (HBV/HCV) 预防计划可以改善检测、治疗 摄取和肝脏相关结果。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 基于社区的筛查举措发现,15.3% 至 34.3% 的筛查个体存在未确诊的 HBV/HCV 感染。综合护理计划检测到 5.3% 至 46.2% 的参与者患有晚期纤维化,3.5% 至 39.2% 的参与者患有肝癌。早期的 诊断 和 治疗 与改善长期肝脏结果相关。在澳大利亚,2015 年至 2022 年间扩大的预防策略估计可预防 969 例 HCV 相关 HCC 病例和 1,427 例 HCV 相关死亡。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 尽管有证据支持预防策略,但医疗保健服务分散、劳动力能力有限、减害服务不足、资金不稳定、患者数据系统不完整以及相互竞争的临床优先事项等障碍限制了计划的有效性。患者层面的障碍,如肝炎意识有限、耻辱、社会经济不稳定以及维持随访困难(失访率从 11.5% 到 39.6%)也影响了护理。

news.content_title: Social participation essential to prevent hepatitis
news.content: Around 10 million (1 crore) people in Bangladesh are living with hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Bangladesh is among the 10 countries with the highest number of hepatitis-related deaths worldwide. The country remains far behind in achieving the goal of eliminating hepatitis by 2030. Participants at a roundtable discussion said that achieving this target will require broad social participation. These observations emerged at a roundtable discussion titled “Hepatitis: Social Participation is essential for prevention and control”, held yesterday, Tuesday, at the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka. The Hepatology Society of Dhaka, Bangladesh, and Prothom Alo jointly organised the event ahead of World Hepatitis Day, observed on 28 July. Speaking as the chief guest, Professor Foara Tasmim, additional director general (Planning and Development) at the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), said, "We cannot solve the hepatitis problem through treatment alone. We must ensure that people do not contract the disease in the first place. We need to raise public awareness, encourage people to protect themselves from infection, and ensure treatment for those who become infected." She added that the DGHS has prioritised hepatitis prevention and is discussing expanding vaccine coverage and ensuring an adequate vaccine supply with Gavi. At the beginning of the discussion, Mohammad Saiful Islam, associate professor in the Department of Liver Diseases at Bangladesh Medical University and Scientific Secretary of the Hepatology Society, cited findings from a study showing that 8.5 million (85 lakh) people in Bangladesh are infected with the hepatitis B virus. Of them, 5.7 million (57 lakh) are men and 2.8 million (28 lakh) are women. Among women of reproductive age between 18 and 45 years, around 1.8 million (18 lakh) are living with the infection, while approximately 400,000 children are affected. Nearly 1.5 million (15 lakh) families in Bangladesh have at least one member infected with the hepatitis B virus. Mohammad Saiful Islam said that around 2.5 million (25 lakh) job seekers and working-age people aged 15 to 30 years are infected with hepatitis B. He noted that many employers automatically declare hepatitis B-positive candidates ineligible for employment, adding, "This is not a scientifically justified practice." The event also highlighted that several types of hepatitis viruses exist, including hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, hepatitis D, and hepatitis E, each causing different forms of the disease. Hepatitis C is a leading cause of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. Ten countries account for 69 per cent of hepatitis C-related deaths worldwide, including China, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Ghana, the Philippines, South Africa, and Vietnam. Mohammad Kamrul Anam, physician at the National Institute of Gastroenterology and Liver Diseases and Hospital and International Affairs Secretary of the Hepatology Society, emphasised the importance of screening and vaccination to prevent hepatitis transmission. He said that all adults living in areas with a high prevalence of hepatitis B should undergo hepatitis testing at least once in their lifetime. He added that people with liver disease, individuals with weakened immune systems, people who use or previously used injectable drugs, prisoners, patients undergoing dialysis, blood or organ donors, healthcare workers, and pregnant women should all undergo hepatitis screening. He then explained the methods used for hepatitis screening and diagnosis. Tanvir Ahmad, assistant professor at Bangladesh Medical University and Media and Publications Secretary of the Hepatology Society, said that hepatitis is preventable, detectable, treatable and, in many cases, can be eliminated. He said that the Hepatology Society organises education and training programmes, workshops, scientific seminars, and conferences for physicians. He also said that the organisation plans to expand nationwide awareness campaigns, conduct targeted screening among high-risk populations, introduce awareness programmes in educational institutions, and strengthen international collaboration. SAM Nazmul Hasan, associate professor in the Department of Liver Diseases at Bangladesh Medical University and Organising Secretary of the Hepatology Society, said the media has five key responsibilities: presenting science-based information; promoting preventive behaviour; encouraging people to undergo screening; highlighting fear, stigma and social discrimination; and playing a constructive role in shaping public health policy. Professor Abdullah Al Mahmud, head of the Department of Liver Diseases at Chattogram Medical College and Founding President of the Liver Care Society, said Bangladesh has been administering the hepatitis vaccine through the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) since 2003. He said everyone born before 2003 should undergo hepatitis screening. He added that surveys have found hepatitis infection rates ranging from 1 to 5 per cent among various occupational groups in Chattogram, including students, salon workers and hospital technicians. Professor Ruknuzzaman, chairman of the Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology at Bangladesh Medical University, said hepatitis A and hepatitis E spread primarily through contaminated food. He noted that street food is one of the major sources of these infections. He added that the hepatitis vaccine effectively protects people against liver cancer and therefore may also be regarded as a cancer-preventing vaccine. Professor Firoza Begum, president of the Obstetrical and Gynaecological Society of Bangladesh (OGSB), said hepatitis B and hepatitis C are among the leading causes of chronic diseases such as liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. She explained that these viruses spread from mother to child as well as from one infected person to another. Transmission from mother to newborn usually occurs during childbirth. She said newborns should receive the hepatitis vaccine within 12 hours of birth to prevent infection. Speaking about the history and significance of World Hepatitis Day, Professor Mohammad Golam Azam, general secretary of the Hepatology Society and Head of the Department of Liver and Gastroenterology at BIRDEM General Hospital, said fatty liver disease can lead to hepatitis. He added that alcohol consumption and certain tuberculosis medications may also cause hepatitis. In his closing remarks, Professor Mohammad Shahinul Alam, chairman of the Department of Hepatology at Bangladesh Medical University and president of the Hepatology Society, said, "The greatest obstacle to preventing or eliminating hepatitis is ignorance and a lack of awareness. Ninety per cent of infected people do not even know that they carry the virus. Around 8.5 million (85 lakh) people in Bangladesh are infected with hepatitis B, while another 1.5 million (15 lakh) are living with hepatitis C. However, treatment is available, and effective medicines exist." He added, "Preventing and controlling hepatitis requires social participation. Social participation means the involvement of all stakeholders, including physicians, the government, the state, the media, professional organisations and researchers." Firoz Choudhury, assistant editor of Prothom Alo, moderated the roundtable discussion
